vulnerability: Arbitrary external call allows unauthorized token minting
reason: The swap function lets any caller specify an arbitrary target and callData, and executes target.functionCall(callData) with the proxy contract as msg.sender. Because the proxy is intended to be a minter/controller for many token contracts, it holds privileged permissions on them. An attacker can set target to a token contract where the proxy has minting rights and set callData to mint tokens to the proxy (or attacker). The proxy will call the token contract, which authorizes the mint because msg.sender is the trusted proxy. To pass the receiveToken balance check, the attacker can mint tokens to the proxy and set receiveToken to the same token, causing the proxy to transfer the newly minted tokens to the attacker. The attacker only needs to send a tiny amount of NATIVE or an ERC20 (amount > 0) to satisfy _checkVaultOut. This results in unlimited minting of any token that grants the proxy minting rights.

vulnerability: Unlimited token approval to arbitrary target allows draining token balances
reason: When tokenAddr is not NATIVE, swap pulls amount from the user and then, if the current allowance to target is less than amount, calls IERC20(tokenAddr).safeApprove(target, MAX_UINT256). Because target is attacker-controlled, an attacker can set it to a malicious contract. After the approval, target.functionCall(callData) is executed. The malicious contract can call tokenAddr.transferFrom(address(this), attacker, tokenAddr.balanceOf(address(this))) to drain the proxy's entire balance of tokenAddr. The attacker only needs to provide at least 1 wei of tokenAddr (which can be flash-loaned) and can use a separate malicious receiveToken to satisfy the balance increase check. This allows theft of all ERC20 tokens held by the proxy, including locked user funds if the proxy acts as the liquidpool.

vulnerability: Arbitrary external call with unlimited approval to user-controlled toAddr allows theft of bridged funds
reason: The function is restricted to controllers, but in a bridge system the controller is typically a relayer that processes user-submitted orders. The user can control the toAddr and data parameters through the cross-chain order. The function transfers amount of tokenAddr to the proxy (or mints it), then approves toAddr for MAX_UINT256 if the allowance is insufficient, and calls toAddr with data. A malicious toAddr contract can use the approval to call tokenAddr.transferFrom(address(this), attacker, tokenAddr.balanceOf(address(this))), draining the bridged amount and any other balance of tokenAddr held by the proxy. It can then satisfy the receiveToken balance check using a token it controls. This allows an attacker to steal the bridged funds and potentially other users' funds if they can influence the controller's call parameters.
